No. "Always" is false, and this plan's weak point is the $5k, not the payoff.

The payoff earns a guaranteed 3.1%, which is roughly what cash or Treasuries yield, so you give up little return. What you give up is liquidity. Home equity can't be spent on a job loss, medical bill, or major repair. A HELOC or cash-out refinance would cost far more than 3.1%, and lenders tighten or freeze credit when the economy is bad or your income stops, which is when you'd need it. $5k covers a few weeks of expenses at best.

Eliminating the mortgage payment does lower your monthly burn, so you need a smaller emergency fund than before. But property tax, insurance, utilities, and maintenance remain, and $5k is still thin.

A better version: pay down only what leaves 6-12 months of post-payoff expenses in cash. Or hold the cash and keep the mortgage, since 3.1% debt costs about what the cash earns.

The full payoff is defensible if you have other liquid assets (brokerage, a sizable taxable account), very stable income or a second earner, and a strong preference for the peace of mind. If $200k is nearly all your liquid net worth, don't do it.
